title: Living in the Faroe Islands | How People Live Where Trees Cannot Grow | 4K
fullText: There is a place where rivers of fog pour over the clifftops and fall toward the sea like water in slow motion. Where driving to work means circling a glowing roundabout deep beneath the Atlantic Ocean. where sheep outnumber people almost 2 to one, where not a single tall tree grows. And yet the population has just reached the highest number in its history. 18 islands in the North Atlantic, 4 hours of daylight in winter, and more than 55,000 people who would not trade this life for any other. This is the Pharaoh Islands. The world says isolation breeds loneliness. These islands have spent a thousand years proving the opposite. And the next 20 minutes will show you how. The day begins at the harbor of Torch Shavven, a few minutes past 5. Most capital cities wake you with a roar of traffic. This one wakes you with the knock of water against wooden hulls, the cry of a few gulls, and the first cafe switching on its lights behind fogged glass. Fishermen in wool caps nod to each other on the dock. Nobody hurries on these islands. Even the capital keeps the pace of a village. Inside that first cafe, the woman behind the counter knows most of her customers by name and knows their order before they reach the till. And yet, this modest little harbor town carries serious weight. On a narrow finger of rock reaching into the bay stands Tinganese. The name means Parliament Point where Norse settlers began gathering to make their laws over a thousand years ago. It remains one of the oldest parliamentary meeting places on Earth. What is remarkable is that nothing about it announces importance. The government of an entire nation works out of small timber buildings painted deep red with grass growing thick on the roofs. A tourist could walk past the prime minister's office and assume it was a fisherman's cottage. And those grass roofs are not decoration. They are a technology older than the parliament itself. A thick living blanket that drinks the rain and holds in the warmth trusted on these islands for a thousand years. In summer, someone still has to climb up and trim the government's rooftops. That smallalness is not a weakness here. It is a design. The prime minister's phone number sits in the public directory and locals will tell you with a shrug, not a boast, that anyone can call. Across all 18 islands, there are only about nine traffic lights, one university, one airport, one television station. Most people here will live their entire lives without ever learning what a traffic jam feels like. In a world where every city seems locked in a race to grow taller, louder, and faster, Torchan made a different calculation. It looked at itself. The harbor, the red timber, the grass roofs, room for everyone who wants to be here, and decided that this was enough, not as surrender, as a choice. And this year, more people are making that choice than ever before. The population of these islands just passed 55,000, the highest in their entire history. In an age when remote villages across Europe are quietly emptying out, this scattered outpost in the middle of the ocean is growing. But the thing that pulls this scattered nation together every morning does not sit on the surface of the land at all. Leave Torchan heading north and the road does something roads are not supposed to do. It bends downward, aims itself at the cold Atlantic and dives straight under it. The walls of rock close in. The radio crackles softly. And somewhere above the roof of your car hangs an entire ocean. The engineers who carved this road did it the hard way. Drilling into solid bassalt, packing the holes with explosives, blasting, clearing, and starting again. Meter by meter, kilometer by kilometer, under the full weight of the North Atlantic. For a minute or two, it feels like an ordinary tunnel. Then the mountain opens. Because at the deepest point of this road, there is something that exists nowhere else on the planet. 72 m beneath the surface of the fjord, the tunnel widens into a roundabout, a traffic circle under the sea. At its center rises a ring of steel figures 80 m around. Human silhouettes holding hands washed in light that shifts from deep blue to green to violet. Drivers call it the jellyfish. It is the work of the pharaoh's artist Tronor Patisonon. And if you tune your radio to 97.0 FM as you circle it, you will hear music composed for this exact place by the pharaoh's musician, Yens L. Thompson. A soundsscape built from the recorded sounds of the tunnel's own construction. A nation put an art gallery and a concert hall at the bottom of the ocean and then drove to work through it. The Easter tunnel opened in December of 2020 and the numbers behind it are almost absurd. around €260 million. The largest single investment in the history of the Pharaoh Islands, made by a nation smaller than a midsized town. Three tunnel branches meeting under the sea. A trip that used to demand more than an hour of driving and sailing now takes 16 minutes. And before the tunnels, that hour was never guaranteed. The ferry meant checking the sky, and the sky meant sometimes you simply did not go. Grandparents here can remember storms that turned a neighboring island into a foreign country for a week. And it is not alone. Four undersea tunnels now thread through the bedrock here. More than 33 kilometers of road carved beneath the seafloor, blasted meter by meter through solid basalt. Today, more than 90% of the population is connected by road. For a thousand years, the sea decided who could reach whom and when, and whether the doctor would arrive in time. These islanders did not wait for the world to fix that. They drilled through the floor of the ocean themselves. 18 islands and they have simply refused to let the word island tell them what they can be. On the far side, the road climbs back into daylight and delivers you to a village where not long ago, the male arrived on foot over a mountain. Gasadalur might be the most photographed village in the North Atlantic. a handful of houses above a waterfall that leaps off the cliff and falls straight into the sea. The waterfall is called Mulafosour and on the windiest days it performs a small act of rebellion. The gusts catch the falling water and throw it back up over the cliff edge. A waterfall running in reverse. Around 18 people live here. Until October of 2004, there was no road at all. The only way in or out was a footpath over a 400 m mountain. And three times every week in wind, rain or snow, the postman climbed it with the village's letters on his back. 4 hours there and home again. The trail is still there, and it still carries his title, the postman's path. Then the islanders did what they always do. They drilled through the mountain. Spend a day out here and you begin to understand the local arithmetic. These islands have three things in endless supply: wind, waves, and sheep. The name Foya itself is usually read as sheep islands and the sheep have earned it. They outnumber the people nearly 2 to one and they roam wherever they please. When a flock decides to stand in the middle of the only road, traffic simply stops. Nobody honks, nobody shouts. The drivers wait, the sheep finish their meeting, and life resumes. 17 of the 18 islands are inhabited, some by thousands of people, some by a family or two. And every one of them runs on that same patience. The wind is less patient. It carries salt from the sea across every hillside. And that salt is one reason you will search these 18 islands in vain for a single tall tree. Rain falls here around 280 days a year. And the locals have a saying that visitors laugh at on day one and repeat seriously by day three. If you do not like the weather, wait 5 minutes. But the missing trees leave behind a real question. One that thousands of viewers of videos like this one have asked. No forests means no firewood. So, how did people on a freezing rock in the North Atlantic keep themselves warm for a thousand years? Hold that question. The answer is waiting a few stops ahead inside the oldest wooden house on Earth. Off the western tip lies Mckinis, the puffin island. In summer, tens of thousands of the little clown-faced birds nest along its cliffs. And from a boat, the rockface itself seems to shiver and move. Not stone, but wings. Out here on islands where a storm can cut the world away for three weeks at a time, there is no such thing as a stranger. When the boats cannot sail, and the helicopter cannot fly, the freezers are counted, the pantries open, and the long evenings filled with card games and old stories told again and improved a little with each telling. The villagers learned centuries ago the only insurance policy that never fails out here, each other. Wind, waves, and sheep can feed a memory. But feeding 55,000 people takes something colder, deeper, and far more valuable. 6:00 in the morning in a fjord so still it mirrors the clouds. A workboat hums between giant floating rings. Beneath each ring circle thousands of Atlantic salmon, swimming against the cold, clean current. An hour north in Claxvik, the fishing capital of the islands. Trawlers unload the night's catch while the town is still half asleep. Claxvvic grew up around its harbor the way other towns grow around a square. This is the engine room of the nation. The numbers it produces are hard to believe. In recent years, these islands have exported around $1.2 $2 billion of seafood annually. Roughly $23,000 for every man, woman, and child. Per person, few fishing nations on Earth come close. Unemployment sits below 3%. Average incomes have climbed higher than in Denmark itself. And all of it rests on a simple philosophy that one local summed up without a hint of drama. Without fish, there is no living here. A view cannot fill a table. So the pharaohs decided long ago to do one thing and to do it better than almost anyone. Controlling the whole chain themselves from the fjord to the fillet to the foreign port. By morning, salmon that slept in a pharaoh's fjord is on its way to restaurant kitchens in Paris and Tokyo. Sold under the island's own name. Cold water, slow growth, premium price. But do not mistake tradition for standing still. The boy who would once have inherited a rowing boat now studies aquaculture engineering or marine biology. Engineers here are testing tidal power in the straits. And thanks to nearly full fiber optic coverage, connection speeds that embarrass most of Europe, a designer can take a video call with London from a grass roof studio while sheep graze outside the window. The islands that once waited weeks for news now move information faster than the cities that used to pity them without changing the view from a single window. The sea gives this nation nearly everything and once a year it also hands them their hardest conversation. For centuries, the grind, the communal drive of pilot whales into the shallow bays, has put food in Pharaoh's storehouses through winters that forgave nothing. To the people here, it is heritage shared out door to door, never sold. To much of the outside world, it is a practice they cannot accept. Both of those sentences are true at the same time. And these islands live in the space between them. Money though only explains how people eat. It has never explained why a thousand years of families refuse to leave. For that you need to visit a black wooden farmhouse at the edge of the water. On the southwestern shore of Stryoy, where the land runs out of excuses and meets the sea, stands the village of Kirk Yubour. The ruined stone walls of a cathedral from the 1200s rise against the sky. And beside them sits a long low farmhouse, black timber, grass roof, red window frames. It does not look like a world record. It is one. This is Kirk Gubber Gador. Built in the 11th century and widely considered the oldest wooden house on earth that has never stopped being lived in. Since the year 1550, it has been home to one family, the Pattersons. The people living there today are the 17th generation. Pause on that number. Since this family took over these rooms, the Ottoman Empire rose and vanished. Kingdoms redrrew every map of Europe. The Soviet Union was born, ruled half the world, and dissolved. And through all of it, in this one house above the same gray sea, one family kept lighting the same fire. 17 generations of storms. 17 generations of Pete smoke curling from the same roof. Which brings us back to the question from the village of Gasadalur. The question of the missing trees. Step inside the oldest part of this house and you find the answer written into its name. The ancient main room is called the Roy Stoa. Translated, it means the smoke room. Step through its low doorway and the centuries close around you. Dark timber walls polished by a thousand years of hands worn plank floors and above the hearth the old opening that let the fire breathe. For most of a thousand years, the fire in that room burned Pete. Bricks of turf cut from the hillsides in spring, stacked and dried in the wind, and carried home for winter. When Pete was scarce, there was driftwood hauled from the beaches. And the timber of this very house, so the old story goes, arrived the same way, drifted and shipped from Norway, already cut and numbered, ready to raise on the little island of Cultur. Families had no pete at all. So they rode to the neighboring islands, cut it there, and fied their winter warmth, homeboat load by boatload. Whale oil lit the lamps. Nothing was wasted because nothing could afford to be. That is how you survive a treeless rock for a millennium. You burn the hillside. You burn what the sea donates and you roof your home with living grass, insulation the Vikings trusted, still breathing with the land today. And the story has one more turn. The grandchildren of the Pete cutters now draw more than half their electricity from wind and water. And the national plan says all of it will be renewable by 2030. From dried turf to turbines, one island logic a thousand years apart. Here a house is not something you buy. It is something you inherit tend and hand on like a name. When the winter dark falls at 3:00 in the afternoon, windows like these begin to glow. And inside this nation does the thing it does best of all. A winter afternoon here is a short silver gray gift, and by 3:00 it is already leaving. This is the hour the islands turn inward. Lamps come on behind small windows. Coffee goes on the stove. In living rooms across the archipelago, knitting needles click through rows of the lapaca. The patented wool sweater whose geometry marks these islands like a signature. Teenagers wear them without irony in the same patterns their greatgrandparents wore because some clothes are simply clothes and some are a flag you can put on. On the good nights, the furniture gets pushed to the walls. People link hands in a long line that curls back on itself and someone begins to sing. This is the Pharaoh's chain dance and it has been performed this way for roughly 800 years. No instruments, no stage, no audience, just human voices carrying the old ballads. The gved verse after verse about warriors and shipwrecks and stubborn love while dozens of feet strike the floor in one shared heartbeat. Children learn the words the way they learn to walk by standing inside the circle. And the chain has no fixed size. On an ordinary night, it might be 20 people in a living room. At the national festival of Olafsa in late July, it becomes thousands, filling the streets of Toshavan past midnight. One voice as wide as a town. The language those ballads protected is itself a survivor. Pharaoh descends straight from old Norse. And for centuries under Danish rule, it was pushed out of schools, out of churches, out of official life. A tongue kept alive behind closed doors, in kitchens, and in song. Today, it is the first language of every child on these islands, spoken by only about 80,000 people on Earth. And it is no museum language. It is the language of text messages and tax forms of laabis and job interviews, a thousand-year-old tongue, doing modern work without complaint. And when the digital age ignored it, the pharaohs answered in the most pharaoh's way imaginable. In 2017, their language was still missing from Google Translate. So, the islanders built their own, a website where anyone in the world could type a phrase and a real volunteer would answer with a live video, translating it themselves, face to camera. The results still sound invented. 1.3 million translations requested from 181 countries and the volunteers doing the translating. 41% of the entire national population. Nearly half a nation signed up unpaid and unasked to be a living dictionary. Google noticed and began work on adding pharaohies. But the point had already been made. This is not a people who wait to be preserved. Keeping a language alive though turns out to be the easy part. Keeping a 22year-old is harder. From the ferry, the island of Kalsoy looks like a dragon sleeping half underwater. A single unbroken spine of mountains 17 km long, threaded by one narrow road, and four tunnels cut through the rock by hand. In the village of Mikladur facing the open sea stands a woman made of bronze and steel. She is the copperan the seal wife 2.6 m tall raised in 2014 by the sculptor Hans Powi Olsen. Legend says the seals were once people and that on the 12th night after Christmas, they come ashore, shed their skins, and dance as humans until dawn. The statue stands where the Atlantic hits hardest and takes the waves without moving. At the island's northern tip under the Calla Lighthouse, a small stone marks the spot where James Bond was filmed and according to the story laid to rest. Film crews found this edge of the world eventually. The pharaohs had been living on it all along. But the real drama of Kausoy is quieter and it sits at every kitchen table on these islands. How do you persuade someone who is 22 that a village of 50 people is enough when the entire world streams through the phone in their pocket. Many leave to Copenhagen for university, to London for careers, and every departure is felt. In a nation this size, one emptied house changes a street. One closed school changes an island. And for years, more of the levers were young women tilting the balance of an already small nation. Out of that reality came something the islands rarely make the news for. Several hundred women from Thailand and the Philippines have moved here, married Pharaoh's men, and become the island's largest minority. Women who traded the tropics for 4 hours of winter daylight. One of them put her verdict simply here. There is no pollution, there is no crime, and I am happy. And then there is the pattern nobody predicted. The ones who left keep coming back. In their 30s with degrees and skills and a taste of everything the big cities promise. They return not because they failed out there but because they finally knew exactly what they were comparing. A person who has lived in both worlds and chooses the 50 person village is not trapped. They are answering a question most of us never get to ask out loud. The proof is in the number this story began with 55,000 people. The most these islands have ever held. The suitcase still opens. But more and more it opens in the arrivals hall. Ask the returners why and the answers rhyme. the children, the safety, the sea, and the feeling of being a person again instead of a password. Every road on this archipelago eventually runs out of land. The last one ends at a lighthouse facing the open Atlantic, and that is where the answer lives. Suduroy is the southernmost island and at its very tip stands the lighthouse of Acraberg, keeping watch since 1909. Beyond it, there is nothing but ocean until the horizon gives up. It is here on the high cliffs that the islands sometimes perform their strangest magic. When the wind and fog agree, a whole river of cloud slides over the cliff edge and pours toward the sea. Hundreds of meters of falling mist, moving slowly, almost politely, like a waterfall, dreamed rather than built. The sheep grazing at the top do not lift their heads. They have seen it 10,000 times before. So why do they stay? Not for ease. The wind will argue with you daily. The dark will lean on you for months. Everyone will know your name, your business, and your grandfather's business. The pharaohs have a word for what they get in return. Hugnadur. It is usually translated as cozy contentment, but it means something quieter and sturdier than happiness. It is the feeling of being exactly where you belong with the storm outside and the right people inside. You cannot buy Hugnadur. You can only build it out of years, out of weather survived together, out of a thousand small evenings that ask nothing of you except that you show up. And here is the secret. This whole journey has been circling. These people do not thrive in spite of the isolation, the weather, and the darkness. They thrive because of them. The storms are the reason neighbors cannot afford to be strangers. The distance is the reason a language of 80,000 speakers refuses to die. The hard winters are the reason one family has tended one fire for 17 generations. Comfort builds convenience. Hardship, it turns out, builds belonging. The young who return are not choosing the past. They are choosing the one thing the fast world still cannot manufacture. A place where they are needed, known, and impossible to replace. Home is not the place that asks nothing of you. Home is the place that is worth everything it asks. The Fog River is still falling as the light fades at Acraberg. Somewhere north in a warm room, a chain of hands is starting the first verse of a very old song. The world keeps asking how fast we can live. 18 islands in the North Atlantic keep asking a better question. What exactly are we hurrying toward? So tell us honestly, would you live here? Say it in the comments. And if you are watching from your own far away corner of the world, tell us what keeps you there. If this journey stayed with you, subscribe. The next quiet corner of the world is already waiting. Heat. Heat.
fullTextVi: Có nơi dòng sông sương mù tràn qua đỉnh vách đá và rơi xuống hướng về biển như nước chuyển động chậm. Lái xe đi làm có nghĩa là đi vòng quanh một bùng binh rực sáng sâu dưới Đại Tây Dương. nơi cừu đông hơn người gần như 2 trên một, nơi không có một cây cao nào lớn lên. Chưa hết, dân số vừa đạt con số cao nhất trong lịch sử. 18 hòn đảo ở Bắc Đại Tây Dương, 4 giờ ánh sáng ban ngày vào mùa đông và hơn thế nữa hơn 55.000 người sẽ không đánh đổi cuộc sống này để lấy bất kỳ cuộc sống nào khác. Đây là Quần đảo Pharaoh. Thế giới nói rằng sự cô lập sinh ra sự cô đơn. Những hòn đảo này đã trải qua hàng ngàn năm chứng minh điều ngược lại. Và 20 phút tiếp theo sẽ chỉ cho bạn cách thực hiện. Ngày bắt đầu tại bến cảng Torch Shavven, lúc 5 giờ vài phút. Hầu hết các thành phố thủ đô đều đánh thức bạn bằng tiếng ồn ào của giao thông. Cái này đánh thức bạn bằng tiếng nước đập vào thân tàu gỗ, tiếng kêu của một vài con mòng biển và quán cà phê đầu tiên bật đèn đằng sau sương mù thủy tinh. Những ngư dân đội mũ len gật đầu chào nhau trên bến tàu. Không ai vội vã trên những hòn đảo này. Ngay cả thủ đô cũng giữ nhịp sống của một ngôi làng. Bên trong quán cà phê đầu tiên đó, người phụ nữ đứng sau quầy biết hầu hết khách hàng của mình theo tên và biết thứ tự của họ trước khi họ đến quầy. Chưa hết, thị trấn cảng nhỏ khiêm tốn này lại có sức nặng rất lớn. Trên một khối đá hẹp vươn ra vịnh là Tinganese. Cái tên này có nghĩa là Điểm Quốc hội nơi những người định cư Bắc Âu bắt đầu tụ tập để đưa ra luật của họ hơn một nghìn năm trước. Nó vẫn là một trong những nơi họp quốc hội lâu đời nhất trên Trái đất. Điều đáng chú ý là không có gì về nó cho thấy tầm quan trọng. Chính phủ của cả một quốc gia được xây dựng từ những tòa nhà gỗ nhỏ được sơn sâu màu đỏ với cỏ mọc dày trên mái nhà. Một khách du lịch có thể đi ngang qua văn phòng thủ tướng và cho rằng đó là túp lều của ngư dân. Và những mái cỏ đó không phải là vật trang trí. Chúng là một công nghệ lâu đời hơn chính quốc hội. Chăn sống dày thấm mưa giữ ấm đáng tin cậy trên những hòn đảo này trong một ngàn năm. Mùa hè vẫn có người trèo lên mái nhà chính phủ. Sự nhỏ bé đó không phải là điểm yếu ở đây. Đó là một thiết kế. Số điện thoại của thủ tướng nằm trong danh bạ công cộng và người dân địa phương sẽ biết bạn với một cái nhún vai, không phải một lời khoe khoang, mà bất cứ ai cũng có thể gọi. Trên khắp 18 hòn đảo chỉ có khoảng chín đèn giao thông, một trường đại học, một sân bay, một đài truyền hình. Hầu hết mọi người ở đây sẽ sống cả đời mà không hề biết giao thông là thế nào mứt có cảm giác như thế nào. Trong một thế giới mà mọi thành phố dường như đang bị cuốn vào một cuộc đua tăng chiều cao, to hơn và nhanh hơn, Torchan thực hiện một phép tính khác. Nó nhìn vào chính nó. Bến cảng, gỗ đỏ, mái cỏ, phòng cho ai muốn ở đây, và quyết định rằng thế là đủ, không phải là đầu hàng, mà là một sự lựa chọn. Và năm nay, nhiều người đưa ra lựa chọn đó hơn bao giờ hết. Dân số của những hòn đảo này vừa vượt qua 55.000 người, cao nhất trong toàn bộ lịch sử của họ. Trong thời đại mà những ngôi làng xa xôi trên khắp châu Âu đang lặng lẽ vắng người, rải rác này tiền đồn giữa đại dương ngày càng lớn mạnh. Nhưng điều kéo cả quốc gia rải rác này lại với nhau mỗi sáng lại không ngồi yên trên bề mặt đất chút nào. Để Torchan đi về hướng bắc và con đường làm điều gì đó mà lẽ ra con đường không nên làm do. Nó cúi xuống, nhắm thẳng vào Đại Tây Dương lạnh giá và lao thẳng xuống dưới. Những bức tường đá khép lại. Chiếc radio kêu lách tách nhẹ nhàng. Và đâu đó phía trên nóc ô tô của bạn treo cả một đại dương. Các kỹ sư xây dựng con đường này đã làm việc đó một cách khó khăn. Khoan vào đá bazan rắn, nhét thuốc nổ vào các lỗ, cho nổ, dọn sạch và bắt đầu lại. Từng mét, từng km, dưới sức nặng toàn bộ của Bắc Đại Tây Dương. Trong một hoặc hai phút, nó có cảm giác giống như một đường hầm bình thường. Thế rồi ngọn núi mở ra. Bởi ở điểm sâu nhất của con đường này, có một thứ gì đó không tồn tại ở đâu khác trên hành tinh. 72 m bên dưới bề mặt vịnh hẹp, đường hầm mở rộng thành bùng binh, một vòng tròn giao thông dưới biển. Ở trung tâm của nó nổi lên một vòng các hình thép xung quanh 80 m. Bóng người nắm tay nhau trong ánh sáng chuyển từ xanh đậm sang xanh lục đến màu tím. Các tài xế gọi nó là sứa. Đó là tác phẩm của nghệ sĩ Tronor Patisonon của pharaoh.
